text:
ATLANTA, Ga. (Atlanta News First) — Doctors and veterinarians are sounding the alarm when it comes to protecting pets and children in extreme heat.

When it is hot outside, it is even hotter inside cars. Temperatures rise rapidly by the minute.

“Within five, 10, 15 minutes, a child can die of heat stroke in a car, and they can be forgotten. It’s hard. It’s hard for me to imagine how you forget your child is in a car, but a lot of us got a lot of stuff going on in our mind,” said Dr. Helena Bentley, a pediatrician and owner of Kid Care Pediatrics.

Dr. Bentley suggested that caregivers leave a purse or shoe in the backseat to remember a child is is in the car.

Dr. Bentley said, “five minutes is never at the manicures, it’s never at the grocery store, and it’s never five minutes. So, wherever you’re parking, it’s going to take five minutes to leave your car to get to where you’re going, so I don’t like that logic.”

The same logic applies to pets.

“When it’s very, very hot outside, like it is now in the 90s, you don’t even have 10 or 15 minutes, you only have a few minutes before it gets to unsafe temperatures,” said Dr. Rachel Morgan at North Cobb Animal Hospital.

Legal consequences can follow for people who leave children or pets inside hot cars.

Cobb County police Monday arrested Miles Dickey for leaving a Rottweiler in a car at Town Center Mall in Kennesaw.

“He looks very distressed, it’s hot. He doesn’t look injured or anything but he is hot,” a 911 caller said. “When I pulled up the car he was already here, and I’ve been here three or four minutes. I can’t imagine how hot that car is right now.”

Cobb County records show Dickey left the dog inside the car for approximately 30 minutes with the car off. The police report indicates the temperature inside reached 148 degrees Fahrenheit. Police said they had to force their way through the driver’s side window, and the dog was hyperventilating and did not have any water.

According to records, Dickey was released on a $2,500 bond.

Dr. Morgan said dogs should have fresh water at all times. She said heavy panting, dark red gums, vomiting, weakness and collapse are signs of heat exhaustion and can be dangerous for dogs.

“What I would do is I would get them to the shade immediately. You want to cool them down with some cool but not ice cold water. So you know you don’t need to put ice cubes in there or anything, just some water straight from the tap, run it over them, but the biggest thing is, of course, to get them into your vet immediately,” Morgan said.

Dr. Morgan said even a car’s pet mode with the AC on full blast can still be risky because how long you will spend away from the car is always uncertain.

Dr. Morgan said, “I would try to adjust plans as much as possible, so you’re not leaving your dog in the car.”

Morgan said different dog breeds can have varying reactions to the heat.

“Your short-faced dogs, your bulldogs, your French bulldogs, your pugs, those are going to be very prone to overheating. For those guys, I would recommend, you know, be very brief with the outside activity this time of year, and definitely keep a close eye on them,” Morgan said.

“Your larger dogs typically, they will not overheat quite as fast as your short-faced dogs, but they can overheat a little bit more quickly than humans,” Morgan added.

Morgan also suggested limiting your time outside during the hottest times of day. She suggested putting the back of your hand on the cement for seven seconds, and if it’s too hot for your hand it’s too hot for a dog’s paws.
